entries.title: ‘Pod Save America’ Is in the Wilderness Too
entries.summary: A media platform once criticized for being too beholden to the Democratic “establishment” now reflects the party’s existential woes.
entries.content:
The hosts of “Pod Save America” skipped their usual programming after then-President Joe Biden faceplanted in his debate with now-President Donald Trump. Instead of outlining an optimistic view of Democrats’ chances, the former Obama administration staffers taped an episode called “A Brutally Honest Debate Recap” about whether the 81-year-old incumbent was fit to run against Trump at all.

The break from party orthodoxy upset some Democratic bigwigs. That included Biden’s deputy campaign manager, Rob Flaherty, who sent a fundraising pitch to supporters after the episode aired, throwing out a veiled insult at “self-important Podcasters” who doubted Biden’s ability to win.

At some point over the course of more than a thousand podcast episodes, though, “self-important” turned into just “important,” no qualifiers.

Now, Democratic operatives widely agree that a candidate’s appearance on the show is unequivocally good for any campaign. A sit-down with the “Pod Save” crew is practically a required stop for any 2028 hopeful, whether to draw attention in a digital environment where people’s focus is getting harder to earn, or to attract organizers and donors who could fuel groundwork IRL.

“Pod Save” ranks among both Spotify’s and Apple Podcasts’ most popular shows in the U.S., and consistently sits among the top 25 podcasts in terms of reach in Edison Research’s quarterly metrics rankings since Trump’s second election. How Democrats use it to hash out their ongoing, heated intraparty debates over wokeness, foreign policy, health care and other issues could play a major role in where the party ultimately lands.

Still, in 2024, the podcasters got their way, but their team fell short: Biden dropped out and Trump won. This prompted reflection from the party, as well as from the podcasters.

“I want to do some personal soul-searching, and the party to do soul-searching to fix this, and to do better next time,” Tommy Vietor, one of the hosts, said at the time.

Nearly two years later, Vietor doesn’t have much to say about the results of that search.
Tommy Vietor (2864x1909, AR: 1.50)“I don’t remember saying that at all,” he told The Washington Sun. “What has that looked like? I don’t know. I don’t have a good answer to that.”

What was once a mainstream, often milquetoast liberal media platform that was criticized for being too beholden to the ever-amorphous party “establishment” now reflects the party’s existential woes.

Its relevance isn’t in question. But the hosts’ qualms with the party’s old guard have apparently resulted in a leftward drift in their content that’s made them divisive within the party.

“They are like men in a midlife crisis who were at the top of a medium that a lot of Dems did not understand,” said Yemisi Egbewole, a former Biden aide and now a fellow with the centrist organization Third Way. “I've watched lots of ‘Pod Save’ where they're critiquing the current Democratic Party and the Democratic establishment, and I just think: ‘Didn't you help construct this for eight consecutive years?’”

***

#Resisting Trump’s first term was the express reason the podcasters, former Democratic communications officials, started the show in January 2017. Vietor, Jon Favreau and Jon Lovett founded progressive media company Crooked Media at the same time, with the hope of building a network that could one day counterbalance the right’s well-funded media apparatus. They take turns hosting the show alongside Dan Pfeiffer, a former senior adviser for Barack Obama.

“We just wanted to create a place where we could have these debates. We are not looking to be the deciders. We're not trying to be judge and jury,” Vietor said. “We’re all going to say what we think, and voice our own personal opinions, but we don’t want to be — in no way are we trying for the show to be a place that's adjudicating, or deciding what’s right and wrong.”

Crooked and its offshoots quickly became an all-inclusive Democratic powerhouse. If the focus was once counterprogramming to Trump’s stronghold over the Republican Party, their strongest leverage today is within their own party.

“They have high-level experience in Democratic politics and strong relationships with decision-makers who represent most of the perspectives in the party,” Andrew Bates, a former Biden spokesperson, said in a text message. “It’s valuable that Democrats who are on different wavelengths can get a fair hearing from ‘Pod Save America’ while at the same time being questioned by campaign veterans who talk like normal people and have a strong sense of conscience.”

The hosts’ positions within the ongoing intraparty war are hard to pin down. And how seriously they seem to think the Democratic Party at large should take their opinions is even harder to articulate — especially ahead of the party’s sure-to-be fiery and likely crowded 2028 presidential primary.
Dan Pfeiffer (2998x1999, AR: 1.50)“The day after the midterms, everyone is going to turn to focus on 2028. There will be fights about policy. There will be fights about the best way to communicate. There will be fights about electability. We’re going to go through all of it,” Vietor told The Washington Sun. “We just want to figure out how to provide a platform to all those candidates to make their pitch, to argue about their perspective versus another.”

Intentionally or not, the podcast’s hosts have found ways to wield their large platform’s influence on the party in recent years, like their post-debate episodes where they openly and forcefully questioned Biden’s viability. Or, more recently, in April, when Favreau grilled Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin over his committee’s butchered and then-unreleased 2024 election autopsy.

“I don't know that the current DNC leadership is the biggest fan of our show,” Vietor told The Washington Sun. The DNC did not respond to a request for comment.

They’ve leaned into the base’s progressive, antiestablishment energy, while also broadcasting pragmatic go-vote, get-involved advice to a country deeply disillusioned with, and deeply distrustful of, just about every major political institution.

Occasionally, the hosts poke at tensions within Democrats’ “Big Tent,” using terminology only someone doused in insular online Democratic discourse would understand. In July, Favreau jokingly introduced notorious centrist poster Matt Yglesias as “the online left’s favorite pundit,” as a spokesperson for “the ‘neolib’ shill faction,” and acknowledged that the show’s audience, as of late, has mainly heard from progressive, antiestablishment candidates hoping to push the party left.

“We haven't really had someone on, at least in a while, make a full-throated case for a center-left politics that emphasizes moderation,” said Favreau on the podcast, explaining the Yglesias appearance. “I know that probably sounds exciting and not at all annoying to many of you.”

It’s hard to find a positive comment on that video. Vietor said he and his co-hosts don’t pay much mind to viewer comments because people tend to take the time to do that out of anger. There seems to be no way for the podcast to make everyone in the party happy.

“We did an interview with Matt Yglesias. People were mad about that. Did an interview with Hasan Piker. People were mad about that,” Vietor said. “Same comments, different perspective. I think it's fine. It's a good thing.”

While the show’s hosts have caught a fair amount of flak for having had Piker — a Twitch streamer who’s stirred heated arguments within the party for his polarizing comments about Israel — on their show multiple times, Vietor acknowledged that Piker holds a valuable role in left-wing media.

“We need more people communicating with more groups of voters on every platform in authentic ways,” Vietor told The Washington Sun.

“Often, it's young men who feel especially estranged from the system, the establishment, from politics, and you know, talk to them about progressive values and prevent them from going down to the other side of the horseshoe and getting red-pilled and ending up watching Nick Fuentes,” he explained of Piker’s audience and influence.

***

Even if it’s not clear what the hosts think the party might, or should, look like by 2028, some listeners have noticed the hosts’ antiestablishment tack.

Longtime Democrats said they identified with the “Pod Save” hosts’ perceived political trajectory, or at least with their frustrations with the party’s status quo.

“They, like many sort of ‘normie Democrats,’ are really pissed at the party. They share a lot of rank-and-file party members' and Democratic primary voters' frustration with ‘the establishment’ — with the gatekeepers, with the old guard,” said Amanda Litman, cofounder of Run For Something, a progressive political organization that recruits and props up younger candidates for down-ballot races, who’s appeared multiple times on the show. “The version of us that has existed up until now has gotten us to this point. This point is bad.”
Jon Favreau,Jon Lovett (2954x1969, AR: 1.50)The show has maintained a particularly powerful platform, Litman said, not only because of the audience’s size, but because it’s chock-full of particularly eager and engaged Democrats. Sure, they might not represent a median voter, but their community — whose paid members are affectionately, parasocially referred to as “Friends of the Pod” — is activated by what they hear.

On the other hand, progressives say the hosts still seem to be grappling with their centrist, politics-as-usual tendencies.

Joe Wrote, the pen name for a Democratic socialist whose media criticism often gains online traction, said he’s noticed, while watching the show and reading viewer feedback, that “it seems like people are pretty solidly to the left of where they are, and they're being pulled along.” To him, the show’s welcoming platform is also its pitfall.

“When you have these politicians on, and you don't hold their feet to the fire or press them on how their beliefs are out of step with the Democratic electorate, then you're not really addressing the tension,” Joe Wrote said. “I think the ‘Pod Save America’ guys and their hosts do think that they can build a better world. I just think that at some point, they do have to ask themselves, ‘Is our theory delivering?’ Right? We spent the last decade telling people to vote, vote, vote. It didn't work.”

The hosts act more as wind vanes than bellwethers, other Democrats agreed.

“A bunch of people that were working within or working with the establishment when that was working for Democrats have seen the establishment fail,” said the digital strategist behind the X account OrganizerMemes, best known for holding workshops to help Democrats create memes for campaigns and progressive causes. “The movement is a different place than it was five years ago, 10 years ago, where a lot of people, I think, are more open to giving the more progressive wing a shot because of the failures.”

After this year’s midterms, which will follow a summer of bitter primaries for Democrats, the party will have only two years to gauge its base’s appetite for change and strategically market a wholesale vision of what a Democratic future can even look like post-Trump.

Trump “upended” American politics as the men had understood them, Vietor acknowledged — and he admits that “the base is getting fed up with the system,” and also that its voters “hate politics, they don’t think it’s working, and they want something different.”

Still, nearly a decade after their first episode, the hosts’ advice on how their listeners can save America remains unchanged.

“If you're frustrated, you know, get in there and change it. That's the only way it works. We — it’s a frustrating answer sometimes, but this is the country we've got. This is the political system we've got,” Vietor said. “And if you want to fix it, you know, roll up your sleeves. Like, that's my answer.”

entries.title: Democratic States and Cities Are Suing to Stop A Public Charge Rule
entries.summary: The rule, set to go into effect mid-September, would allow officers to consider immigrants' use of public benefits when making visa decisions.
entries.content:
More than 20 Democratic-led states and several cities are announcing lawsuits Monday to stop the Trump administration from considering immigrants’ use of public benefits when deciding whether they qualify for permanent legal status.

New York Attorney General Letitia James is leading 20 states, the District of Columbia and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro in one legal challenge. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is leading Chicago, San Francisco, Seattle, and two counties, Santa Clara County in California and King County in Washington, in a separate case.

In July, the Department of Homeland Security published a final rule, set to go into effect on Sept. 18, that greatly widened the scope of what officers could consider when looking at public charge. Now, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services officers have few guardrails about what benefits they can consider, including an applicant's health or prior use of public assistance.

“Hardworking families should not be forced to go without the support they need because they fear asking for assistance will get them deported,” James wrote in a statement. “This rule preys on that fear and counts on families forfeiting the food assistance, health care coverage, and other public benefits to which they are legally entitled.”

The DHS rule reverses a Biden-era policy that had restricted the consideration of public charge to consider only cash welfare.

President Donald Trump tried to make similar changes to public charge during his first term, before a group of Democratic states sued over the changes. James filed a lawsuit in conjunction with New York City, Connecticut and Vermont at that time as well, which succeeded in blocking the enactment of the rule.

Both of the new lawsuits claim that the rule would cause undue hardship and burden to state and local governments, and that DHS wants to exceed the agency’s authority.

“The new public charge rule seeks to push immigrant families away from the programs that have kept people fed and healthy for decades,” Mamdani said in a statement. “That fear will not stop at the families that the federal government is targeting. Families who remain fully eligible for benefits will feel a chilling effect, and all New Yorkers will pay for it.”

entries.title: Trump Cuts Irish Whiskey Tariffs Because ‘Everyone’s Been Bugging Me’ About It
entries.summary: He made the surprise announcement at the trophy ceremony for the Irish Open.
entries.content:
By Darlene Superville and Jill Lawless

DOONBEG, Ireland (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Sunday at the close of a golf tournament in Ireland that he plans to remove a 10% tariff on Irish whiskey.

Trump said during the trophy ceremony for the Irish Open that he had been asked about the issue by everyone, including Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin and even some of the golfers. Irish Open winner Shane Lowry was among them, Trump said.

“Everybody’s been bugging me” to do it, the Republican president said. “And I said, ‘On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off'" of Irish whiskey.

Irish whiskey currently faces the standard tariff imposed by Trump on most imports from the European Union, which was reduced from 15% to 10% in July.

Trump announced in April that he was lifting certain tariffs on U.K. whiskey, which includes Scotch and spirits made in Northern Ireland, creating an imbalance with Ireland.

Trump’s surprise announcement was met with loud whistling and cheers from the crowd of spectators. Details on how soon the tariff would be lifted were not immediately available.

Chris Swonger, president & CEO of the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States, called Trump's announcement “another positive step toward reducing barriers to spirits trade” and said everyone would benefit from it during the coming holidays.

“As U.S. hospitality businesses enter the critical holiday season, this action will provide a welcome boost for retailers, restaurants, consumers and the American economy,” Swonger said.

In May, the Irish Whiskey Association called for the tariffs to be removed, arguing that such a step would help many U.S. companies with Irish products in their portfolios and avoid uncertainty for consumers.

Trump said on April 30 that he gave the United Kingdom a tariff break on whiskey after King Charles III and Queen Camilla visited the White House. “The King and Queen got me to do something that nobody else was able to do, without hardly even asking!” Trump posted on social media.

The Scotch Whisky Association said July 24 that the zero-tariff policy had come into effect.

entries.title: Stefon Diggs Scores in D.C. Debut, But His Celebration Proves Costly
entries.summary: Diggs was flagged for unsportsmanlike conduct after his fourth-quarter touchdown, preventing Washington from going for two.
entries.content:
Stefon Diggs picked the wrong time to go for a hug.

The Maryland native had a respectable debut for his hometown team Sunday, catching four passes for 55 yards against the Eagles with a fourth-quarter touchdown. But Diggs’ celebration proved to be costly, as it prevented the team from attempting to tie the game early in the fourth quarter.

The Commanders fell to the Eagles, 24-22, after a failed two-point conversion with 1:01 left in the game. But Diggs deprived his team of another two-point try earlier in the quarter. After connecting with Jayden Daniels on a 10-yard pass for his first Commanders touchdown, Diggs launched himself into the goal post and hugged it, immediately drawing a 15-yard penalty for unsportsmanlike conduct. (Any contact with the goal post results in a penalty.)

The flag cost the Commanders a chance to go for two at that point, which coach Dan Quinn said he would have done. Ultimately, the Commanders hit a 48-yard extra point to make the score 17–16.

“I take full accountability,” Diggs told reporters after the game. He added that the Commanders’ offensive struggles through the first three quarters had frustrated him, which caused him to overcelebrate on the touchdown.

“When we clicked after not clicking for a little while, it got to me a little.”

Diggs, who also starred at Maryland, led the team in targets in the game with nine, and finished second in yards to rookie wide receiver Antonio Williams, who had four catches for 64 yards and the touchdown that set up Washington’s failed two-point conversion at the end of the game. (Washington’s primary pass catcher, Terry McLaurin, caught just two passes for 14 yards on four targets.)

The 32-year-old signed with his hometown team after spending last season with the AFC champion Patriots, catching 85 passes for 1,013 yards. He was released in March while facing charges of strangulation, assault and battery over a dispute with his former private chef. He was found not guilty in May and cleared by the NFL in June of any punishment in relation to its personal conduct policy.

entries.title: Second Federal Judge Freezes Trump’s Mail-in Ballot Order
entries.summary: The ruling adds another obstacle to the administration's effort to rewrite election rules as the Supreme Court is poised to weigh in on the matter.
entries.content:
A federal judge late Sunday ordered that the U.S. Postal Service not implement President Donald Trump's executive order limiting mail balloting, adding another obstacle to the administration's effort to rewrite election rules as the Supreme Court is poised to weigh in on the matter.

The nation's highest court already is considering the administration's appeal of an order by U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani in Boston prohibiting the Postal Service from enforcing its new rule on mail voting before this year's midterm elections.

Late Sunday, U.S. District Judge Carl J. Nichols in Washington, D.C., handed down a similar hold on the rule, which was issued Aug. 21.

“Plaintiffs have demonstrated that, absent an injunction, there is an increased risk that a significant number of otherwise appropriate absentee or mail-in ballots will ultimately not be counted in the upcoming elections,” Nichols wrote in issuing the preliminary injunction. “The public has a strong interest in ensuring that doesn’t happen.”

Nichols in May had refused to issue an injunction because he ruled the lawsuit seeking one was brought too early. That was the high court's reasoning late last month when it lifted an earlier freeze by Talwani. But because the administration had just issued its rule to move ahead with Trump's plan, the plaintiffs in Boston and Washington, D.C., refiled their lawsuits.

Talwani was nominated by former President Barack Obama and Nichols was nominated by Trump.

The new Postal Service regulations stem from an executive order Trump issued earlier this year. Election officials say it would be impossible to implement the changes this close to a general election.

The regulations would require all ballot envelope designs to be pre-approved by the Postal Service and that states upload the identities of those who are to receive them into a still-inactive online portal. Mail ballots already are being sent out in at least three states — Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin — and more states are preparing to distribute mail ballots this week.

A whistleblower report to Congress warned that millions of people would be disenfranchised if the rule was allowed to take effect for the midterms. The union representing U.S. Postal Service workers has pushed back against the executive order, saying it is not the job of postal workers to verify voter eligibility.

Mail balloting has long been a favorite target for Trump, who has falsely blamed it for his 2020 loss to Democrat Joe Biden and claimed it is a pathway to fraud despite his own use of the voting method.

entries.title: Texas Landowners Sue to Stop Trump From Building a Wall Through Big Bend
entries.summary: The lawsuit was filed by Conserve Big Bend and six landowners.
entries.content:
By Rebecca Santana

MARFA, Texas — Landowners, ranchers and business owners in the Big Bend region of Texas along with a nonprofit organization dedicated to protecting the region's landscape and heritage are suing to stop the Trump administration's plans to build a wall and other border infrastructure through the remote section of the state.

The lawsuit, filed by Conserve Big Bend and six landowners and with the support of dozens more people along the border, comes as the administration is ramping up a $46 billion effort to line the roughly 2,000-mile southern border with a collection of 30-foot (9-meter) steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers, and technology intended to keep out smugglers and migrants.

In Texas, the effort has run up against numerous lawsuits and bipartisan opposition from sheriffs, elected officials, tour guides, environmental groups and landowners.

Officials backing the wall “were woefully unprepared for the hornet’s nest they stirred up because they had no idea how much we love this place,” said David Keller, an archaeologist and historian who specializes in the Big Bend and lives in the region.

“For us, the Big Bend is not an empty place on the map,” he said at a press conference announcing the suit. “It is our home.”

As part of its wall-building efforts, the administration has waived numerous regulations and statutes designed to protect the environment, archaeology or wildlife, on the basis that there's an urgent need to protect the border in what Homeland Security has called areas of “high illegal entry.”

But in the lawsuit announced Monday, the plaintiffs argue that when it comes to the Big Bend region, that's not an accurate description. They've cited historical statistics issued by Customs and Border Protection showing how few people cross the border in Big Bend compared with other areas along the U.S.-Mexico border.

Big Bend has about 500 miles of border — roughly one quarter of the total length of the border with Mexico from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico. But the region only accounted for about 1% of arrests, according to the lawsuit’s stats.

Laura Allen, whose family's ranch would have border wall cut right through it under the plans, noted that illegal border arrests have plunged even further since Trump returned to office.

“Thank you, President Trump. You’ve secured the border,” Allen, a two-time Trump voter and former county judge, said at the press conference. "But now let it go. It’s time.”

The plaintiffs are arguing that the Department of Homeland Security is misusing powers from Congress that allow the secretary broad authority to waive regulations in order to build border walls or other infrastructure in areas where there are large numbers of people trying to cross into the country illegally.

“That determination is legally and factually unsound and unsupported,” the plaintiffs wrote.

The lawsuit filed Monday is the latest in efforts to slow or stop the administration's plans in Texas and elsewhere.

The biggest outcry has come over Customs and Border Protection's plans for the Big Bend National Park, which sits in a far southwestern corner of Texas where the Rio Grande separates the U.S. from Mexico.

The park's remote and rugged location, its steep limestone canyon walls and crystal clear starry night views attract visitors from around the world. The government has said in court hearings that no final plans have been decided for what will be built in the park but plans made public so far have included building a new road, installing detection technology and barriers to stop vehicles from crossing the border.

When bulldozers were spotted clearing land in the park in August, people across the state were outraged. CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott temporarily paused construction-related activity in the park but many activists and local residents would like to see even more changes to the administration's plans in the broader Big Bend region.

Native American groups have argued that the construction could inhibit their ability to practice their faith and is damaging important religious sites while environmentalists worry the wall will cause flooding or keep animals from migrating.

Landowners who've lived and worked along the Rio Grande for years have questioned how they'll feed livestock or water their crops if they can't access the river.

___

AP reporter Tim Sullivan in Minneapolis contributed to this story.

entries.title: Judge Rules Trump Administration Must Give The Washington Sun USAID Records
entries.summary: The ruling comes after The Washington Sun sued the government for not responding to a Freedom of Information Act request.
entries.content:
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to release thousands of internal records maintained by the U.S. Agency for International Development, which President Donald Trump has sought to shutter.

U.S. District Judge Amir H. Ali ruled Thursday that USAID “shall produce records at a rate of 500 pages per month” to The Washington Sun. In March, The Sun, which at the time was known as NOTUS, sued the federal government, arguing that it illegally withheld records that are subject to the Freedom of Information Act.

The Sun’s lawsuit stems from a FOIA request Washington Sun Senior Editor Dave Levinthal filed with USAID in November 2024.

The request seeks records detailing how USAID officials anticipated and reacted to the results of the 2024 U.S. presidential election. Shortly after becoming president in January 2025, Trump oversaw the dismantling of USAID, an agency founded during the Kennedy administration that was — until recently — the world’s largest foreign aid agency.

"The court's ruling is a clear signal that the public has a right to observe the inner workings of a government agency the president is dismantling," Washington Sun Editor-in-Chief Tim Grieve said. "We're committed to fighting for these records until we get them."

By law, USAID had 20 working days after receiving Levinthal’s FOIA to disclose the scope of the responsive documents it would produce and to detail any plans to withhold documents under legal exemptions.

But until The Sun sued USAID, the agency had done neither. It also routinely ignored requests for updates and status reports. The agency, which in a court filing this month acknowledged possessing “4,707 potentially responsive records,” continues to withhold all records responsive to the request.

The case is titled NOTUS Media LLC & Levinthal v. U.S. Agency for International Development. Law firm Ballard Spahr LLP is representing The Sun.

For press inquiries, email communications manager Thuy Lan Nguyen: thuylannguyen@washsun.com.

entries.title: DHS Watchdog Says Detainees Were Put in Small Cages at 'Alligator Alcatraz'
entries.summary: The Office of the Inspector General described the practice as unlike anything its inspectors had witnessed at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility.
entries.content:
Staff at Florida’s now-shuttered detention center dubbed “Alligator Alcatraz” put immigrants inside small metal cages they labeled as “calming areas,” according to a report from the Department of Homeland Security inspector general.

The DHS watchdog said 79 detained immigrants spent several minutes to nearly two hours enclosed in the cages. At least two of those were outdoors and didn’t have enough space for someone to lay down, the report published Monday states.

The Office of the Inspector General described the practice as unlike anything its inspectors had witnessed at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility. Florida opened the center in July 2025.

“The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment.” the report states. “Facility staff described the small metal enclosures as ‘calming areas’ for detainees to deescalate and have time alone. Staff further maintained that detainees asked to spend time in the small metal enclosures.”

The existence of the cages was described in an Amnesty International report in December, and The Washington Sun spoke that month with detainees who witnessed others being put in “the box.”

“The mosquitoes were huge. And if someone tells you they’ll put you in the cage, you immediately get scared,” Rogelio Enrique Bolufé Izquierdo, a Cuban national who has since been deported to Ecuador, told The Sun in December.

The outdoor metal cages were 4 feet 3 inches by 4 feet 3 inches and 7 feet 9 inches tall, according to the DHS OIG report.

Gov. Ron DeSantis announced in June the closure of the detention center in the Everglades, nearly a year after it opened. The facility had prompted several lawsuits from environmental and immigration advocacy groups and the Miccosukee Tribe.

The OIG team inspected the lockup in January, finding that it didn’t comply with medical care, food service, personal hygiene and other standards, according to the report. For example, detainees were only allowed to shower three times a week. There was also an insect infestation in the shower facilities.

DHS skirted responsibility for the conditions at Alligator Alcatraz, responding in a letter to the watchdog that it didn’t have a contract with the state to manage the detention space.

“Even as to a facility where a state detains aliens under 287(g) authority, the state maintains authority over the day-to-day operations of that facility,” ICE acting director David Venturella and Brian Cavanaugh, the under secretary for management at DHS, wrote in a letter.

DeSantis’ office and the Florida Division of Emergency Management did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

entries.title: Donald Trump Jr.’s Wife Confirms Lavish Wedding Weekend Was Bankrolled by Russian Oligarch
entries.summary: Bettina Anderson described Umar Kremlev, who has documented ties to Vladimir Putin, as a “dear friend.”
entries.content:
A Russian oligarch financed significant parts of Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding weekend in the Bahamas, his wife confirmed on social media Monday while attempting to brush off concerns about any conflicts of interest the arrangement raised.

“It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful,” Bettina Anderson posted on Instagram. “Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift.”

Trump Jr. married Anderson, a Palm Beach socialite, during a lavish three-day affair at a pair of private islands, with guests put up in oceanfront villas.

But ProPublica reported early Monday morning that Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch with documented ties to President Vladimir Putin, put hundreds of thousands of dollars toward the wedding weekend.

Kremlev rented out a private island, put on a firework show and even had his team help plan the festivities for the president’s son and now daughter in-law, according to the investigative publication.

Anderson asserted that the multiday celebration was “never intended” to be their wedding weekend, and they only decided to get married that Friday because their plans changed. It’s unclear why the distinction would alleviate the conflict of interest concerns raised by the arrangement with Kremlev.

President Donald Trump notably did not attend the festivities.

A spokesperson for Trump Jr. did not dispute the wedding payments in a statement to ProPublica, though they claimed that Kremlev is “not someone he [Trump Jr.] has a business relationship with.”

The intimate guest list of around 50 people included Trump Jr.’s brother-in-law Jared Kushner, his brother Eric Trump and a comparatively large group of Russian guests, whose presence perplexed the other attendees, ProPublica reported.

Despite the limited invite list, Eric Trump’s spokesperson told ProPublica he has absolutely “no clue who this person is, nor has never heard his name” when asked about Kremlev.

Trump Jr. had emphasized the private nature and small guest list for the weekend several times on his podcast, saying it was just “really close friends” and “if you’re on that list, you weren’t talking.”

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida), who has campaigned with Trump Jr. and appeared on his podcast, jumped to the couple’s defense on Monday, calling the reports “gross attacks.”

“To be clear, these attacks come only a few days after the attacks on @jaredkushner regarding the peace negotiations. The fact is that this administration is actively pursuing a peace deal with Russia and Ukraine, and there are MANY people who DON’T WANT this deal to happen. So, they are now resorting to attacking @POTUS’ children,” Luna wrote Monday on X.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California), the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, is demanding answers about potential conflicts of interest related to the wedding weekend. “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers,” Garcia wrote on X.

Kremlev is the head of the once Russian-state financed International Boxing Association and was reportedly part of the delegation that accompanied Russian President Vladimir Putin to China just days before the wedding weekend — though a representative for Kremlev told Propublica that he was not a part of Putin’s "official delegation” on the trip.

Kremlev’s press office calls him a businessman and philanthropist and said he “has never discussed political matters with any of his American friends and acquaintances,” including the president’s son.

Kremlev is currently sanctioned by the Ukrainian government over his ties to Putin, specifically because he is “close friend of the head of Putin's security service.” Ukraine also called out Kremlev for his advocacy for Russian athletes who have been barred from international competitions and noted that he had received a medal by Putin’s decree in 2020 for “his great contribution to the development of physical culture and sports.”

The hundreds of thousands of dollars in wedding payments came from IB Challenger, an entity linked to the boxing association that Kremlev set up in Dubai as Europe became more hostile to Russian businesses.

When asked if Kremlev’s documented ties to Putin raised any concerns, the White House sent The Washington Sun the link to Anderson’s Instagram post.

“We are fortunate to have wonderful friends from all over the world, and we will never be embarrassed or apologetic about being grateful for them,” Anderson wrote in her Instagram post.

entries.title: Trump Asks Smithsonian to Install ‘Colossus’ Statue of George Washington
entries.summary: The proposed statue would be 30 feet tall and stand outside the National Museum of American History.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump is calling on the Smithsonian to replace a decades-old sculpture outside the National Museum of American History with a “colossus” statue honoring George Washington.

Trump wrote in a Truth Social post Friday night that he is asking the Smithsonian to honor the nation's first president with a 30-foot statue ahead of Washington's 300th birthday in 2032. The statue would replace the abstract “Infinity” sculpture, which has welcomed visitors at the museum’s entrance since 1967.

“Replace a sculpture that says nothing about America with the man who, more than anyone else, says everything about America,” Trump said in the post.

Along with the statue, Trump also asked the institute to create a five-year exhibit dedicated to the first president and to install the 11-foot statue of Washington created for the Freedom Grand Prix race in August in the museum's Flag Hall. That statue should be in place no later than Constitution Day on Sept. 17, the post said.

The demands are the latest in Trump’s attempt to control the Smithsonian despite having no direct oversight of the independent agency. The Smithsonian has become part of the culture war during Trump’s second term as the president pushes back against what he calls “a revisionist movement.”

Trump has accused the Smithsonian of casting American history in a negative light. In a March 2025 executive order, he criticized the institution as promoting a narrative “driven by ideology rather than truth.” The Trump administration later launched a review of exhibitions at multiple Smithsonian museums, ultimately publishing a list of exhibitions it found objectionable.

Lonnie Bunch, secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, has defended the agency’s independence through it all. He announced last week he would step down by the end of the year.

In another Truth Social post Friday, Trump bashed “recently ended leadership” at the Smithsonian for giving too much attention to oppressed groups and not enough to people who overcame challenges.

“Instead of focusing on ideological activism, the leaders of America’s taxpayer-funded, National History Museum should be focused on telling America’s story — fairly, accurately, and coherently — and there is no better person to start with than George Washington,” Trump wrote.

entries.title: Trump Says He's the Only Guardrail Needed for Artificial Intelligence
entries.summary: The comments follow Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s calls over the weekend to slow down AI development until proper safety measures catch up.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said Monday that his presidency is the only regulation needed for artificial intelligence, doubling down on previous statements that the United States needs to rush to develop advanced AI tools to beat China at what he sees as an existential competition.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” the president posted on Truth Social. “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies! There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”

He also said the push to regulate AI was a “hoax” equivalent to the twin impeachment efforts during his first term as president, and urged tech leaders to change their minds on the issue. 

“AI, and Data Centers, will be the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History ­­— Bigger than Oil, Gold, Diamonds, or even the Internet. It will not be stopped by brilliantly run Destructive Forces during the Term of President DONALD J. TRUMP!” the post read.

The comments follow Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s calls over the weekend to slow down AI development until proper safety measures catch up with the fast growing autonomous systems. Without such measures, Amodei warned that AI “could be capable of taking over the entire internet” within six to 12 months.

Other tech leaders, including Elon Musk and Open AI CEO Sam Altman, have also called for greater caution.

But the Trump administration is not backing down from what it considers a national security issue and an economic competition with China. Vice President JD Vance told reporters on Monday that the administration was “thoughtful” about the risks of AI, while downplaying industry concerns.

“I feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them,” Vance said. “It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse.”

Concerns over AI regulation and data centers have also become a central issue on the campaign trail ahead of this year’s midterm elections. The president has staunchly defended data centers despite growing voter opposition to projects that residents fear could drive up electricity costs, consume large amounts of water and reshape their communities.

That backlash has already led to projects being rejected or withdrawn in states including Ohio, Georgia, Indiana, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, while state and local officials across the country have moved toward moratoriums, tighter regulations and changes to tax incentives for the industry.

entries.title: Two D.C. Landlords Settle Rent Inflation Lawsuit for $9.3 Million
entries.summary: JBG Smith and Mid-America Apartments were accused of conspiring to keep rents "artificially high."
entries.content:
Two D.C. landlords have agreed to pay $9.3 million to resolve claims that they “illegally conspired” to inflate rents across the thousands of apartments they own across the city, D.C. Attorney General Brian L. Schwalb said in a Monday press release.

It’s the biggest settlement to date in an ongoing series of suits between the D.C. attorney general’s office and 14 local landlords accused of using RealPage software to inflate rental prices at tens of thousands of apartments across the District, which resulted in renters paying millions of dollars more than they should have. Since 2025, three D.C. landlords have settled for a total of $2.4 million. Similar lawsuits have been filed in states including Maryland.

The latest to settle are Tennessee-based Mid-America Apartments, which will pay $1.2 million for allegedly inflating rents at the Post Massachusetts Avenue in Northwest D.C., one of its 269 District properties, and Bethesda-based giant JBG Smith, which owns more than 4,500 units in D.C. JBG Smith will pay $8.1 million to settle claims it inflated rents at multiple properties including The Batley in Northeast D.C., and West Half located in Southeast.

RealPage’s rental software, which uses confidential pricing data from landlords to estimate supply and demand and generate an inflated rental price, is widely employed across D.C. properties: More than 30% of apartments in buildings with five or more units and 60% in buildings with more than 50 units have been priced using it, the attorney general’s office said in its news release.

“This leaves many District residents with no choice but to pay inflated rents,” the office said.

Impacted residents will get some of their money back through a claims administration process, though some of the settlement will go to civil penalties and legal fees. Going forward, landlords will be prohibited from using these tools to artificially inflate rents.

It’s the latest headache for JBG Smith, which has about $2.6 billion in debt tied to its properties, according to its first-quarter Securities and Exchange Commission filings for 2026.

The company was ordered to pay $356 million in damages last month for misrepresenting a condo building it owns in Woodley Park, The Washington Business Journal reported. In May, The Washington Sun reported on a property co-owned by JBG Smith where tenants face abysmal housing conditions with little redress.

Conditions at that property, The Gale Eckington, have not improved since May, and management continues to be unresponsive, one tenant told The Sun. Landlords JBG Smith and Jonathan Rose Companies still owe more than $216,000 for 208 unresolved code violations at the property, according to a public Department of Buildings dashboard.

A spokesperson for JBG Smith said in a statement that the company did not have additional comment at this time, and referred questions about the distribution of settlement funds to the attorney general’s office.

This story was updated with a response from JBG Smith.

entries.title: Kennedy Center Board Lists 10 Options for Putting Trump’s Name on the Building
entries.summary: Without public recognition, the board said Trump is unlikely to help the center.
entries.content:
The Kennedy Center’s Board of Trustees is considering 10 different ways to recognize President Donald Trump on the building’s facade as part of what it says is an effort to secure his fundraising prowess for the performing arts center’s renovation.

The options, outlined in a draft board resolution reviewed by The Washington Sun, would place language recognizing Trump on the exterior marble beneath the Kennedy Center’s name.

“The Board seeks to provide multiple options so that President Trump can be legally and appropriately recognized and acknowledged on the facade of the Kennedy Center so that he agrees to carry the burden of managing the renovation and provides the Center with a much required financial rescue,” the resolution reads.

The proposals range from relatively straightforward acknowledgements of Trump’s support to language crediting him with overseeing the center’s renovation and restoration.

One option would read: “Renovation and endowment overseen by President Donald J. Trump and the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.” Another would say: “With Gratitude for Support from President Donald J. Trump and the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.”

Other proposals would credit Trump with directing or overseeing the renovation, while several would describe the center as being sustained through his “generosity.” One option reads, “A Legacy protected through the Generosity of President Donald J. Trump.”

The board’s draft resolution says the Kennedy Center is facing an imminent financial crisis and has exhausted its fiscal resources, putting its ability to meet payroll and routine maintenance obligations at risk within weeks.

Trump, according to the resolution, has offered to raise the money needed to keep the center from bankruptcy while it undergoes a major renovation.

The board says it believes Trump’s financial support is tied to giving him an appropriate public acknowledgement. The resolution says that without such recognition, Trump is unlikely to provide the oversight of the renovation or lead the center’s financial rescue.

The proposals come as a federal court prepares to consider an emergency motion from Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio member of the board, that seeks to block the Kennedy Center board from again adding Trump’s name to the building.

In December, after the president stocked the board with allies and made himself chairman, the trustees voted for the first time to rename the center after Trump. In August, the board voted once again to add the president’s name, this time opting to inscribe it into the marble facade after a federal judge ordered the previous signage had to be removed.

This week’s hearing is scheduled for 10 a.m. Tuesday, shortly before the board is set to meet and vote on resolutions concerning the center’s future, including possible closure and the proposed Trump recognitions.

The draft resolution says the board intends to pursue “all legal means” to carry out one or more of the proposed recognitions, subject to the board’s vote.

entries.title: Trump Scraps Biden-Era Climate Pollution Rules for Power Plants
entries.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency is proposing going further to eliminate all greenhouse gas standards.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is gutting regulations on climate-warming emissions from coal and gas-fired power plants, the Environmental Protection Agency announced Monday.

The announcement scraps the majority of the EPA’s Biden-era standards that sought to limit greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel plants. New coal and gas-fired plants would still be subject to some 2015 standards, and one Biden-era standard for new gas plants.

At the same time, the agency is proposing to repeal all remaining greenhouse gas emissions standards for power plants and remove the EPA’s ability to impose pollution controls going forward.

The rollback of standards for power plants is the latest EPA action to remove emissions controls across sectors. The Trump administration has erased vehicle emissions standards, repealed the “endangerment finding” that underpins all EPA regulations on emissions, rolled back rules limiting mercury and air toxins, and relaxed restrictions on highly potent greenhouse gases.

“It is part of an agenda that Lee Zeldin has been implementing to strip back EPA's mission regulating all forms of air pollution,” Zealan Hoover, a former EPA adviser for the Biden administration, said of the agency’s current administrator. “That's going to quite directly lead to hundreds of thousands of avoidable deaths.”

Power plants are the largest industrial source of greenhouse gas emissions in the United States and represent a quarter of the country’s total emissions. If the U.S. power sector was its own nation, it would emit more carbon pollution than all other countries except for China, India, Russia.

Monday’s finalized rule means coal-fired power plants will no longer be required to control their carbon pollution using carbon capture and storage technology or by switching some energy generation to natural gas. New gas-fired plants will also see emissions requirements relaxed.

When carbon pollution standards were finalized in 2024, the Biden administration said they were projected to result in $370 billion in benefits, between savings in health care costs and costs associated with climate change. In 2035 alone, they were expected to prevent 1,200 premature deaths.

The Trump administration says repealing the standards would increase coal production tenfold, and save energy companies and tax payers $310 billion over two decades.

The rollbacks do not affect standards for hazardous air pollutants or criteria pollutants — common air pollutants that can harm human health. But in an EPA regulatory impact analysis, emissions of particulate matter, nitrogen oxide, sulfur dioxide and mercury are projected to increase if all emissions standards disappear, compared to a baseline with carbon pollution standards.

The agency has stopped quantifying the benefits of limiting air pollution from ozone and fine particulate matter. An agency analysis says repealing all greenhouse gas standards could result in more additional premature deaths. Estimates based on a snapshot of years vary from 1,200 to 2,700 additional premature deaths.

Zeldin said emissions standards for power plants amounted to a “war on coal,” and that the repeal would help make energy more affordable.

“Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning. We are working to go even further so that American energy can be fully unleashed. Realizing the full potential of American energy means more jobs, lower prices, and a more prosperous America,” he said.

The agency argues greenhouse gas emissions from power plants are out of its scope of responsibility because they have “no material impact” on climate change, and potential public health harms from those emissions are “uncertain, conjectural, remote and convoluted.”

Vickie Patton, general counsel for the Environmental Defense Fund, said this summer’s heat, wildfire smoke and drought demonstrate the need for regulation.

“There's an enormous, long foundation in law that's gone to the U.S. Supreme Court in a number of cases that has held that EPA has the authority and the responsibility to protect American people from dangerous climate pollution,” she said. “To try to walk away from that solemn responsibility is contrary to law, it’s contrary to the science, it’s also contrary to our lived human experiences.”

Patton said her organization feels an “urgent” need to act on the rollbacks, as power plants pop up across the country to fuel the buildout of AI data centers.

EPA officials said the proposal to eliminate all greenhouse gas emission regulations for power plants would be open for public comments for 45 days.

entries.title: Trump Eyes World War II Memorial as Next Makeover Project
entries.summary: The Department of the Interior took a first step toward revamping the World War II Memorial on the National Mall.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is eyeing more D.C. monuments as clean-up targets in an effort to reshape the nation’s capital.

The Department of the Interior has initiated the process to revamp the World War II Memorial on the National Mall, seeking a contractor to clean granite elements, waterproof fountains, replace plumbing systems and address other deferred maintenance, according to a solicitation notice from the agency posted Monday.

President Donald Trump called for repairs to the monument earlier this year.

The monument features granite columns representing each U.S. state and territory at the time of the war, surrounding a pool filled with fountains. The 22-year-old memorial hasn’t been substantially rehabilitated since its construction, and many aspects have begun to deteriorate, according to the notice. But the memorial was closed for construction from January to May for a $3.7 million renovation, which included work on the fountains and lighting, according to the National Park Service.

Trump made his first calls to refine the WWII Memorial in the midst of work on the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, saying the bottom of the WWII fountain was “in pretty bad shape" and should be repainted. He said the color at the bottom of the fountain would be lighter than the reflecting pool’s “American flag blue.” The botched Reflecting Pool resurfacing cost more than $14 million and took more than 60 days to complete. The new paint started peeling off the bottom of the pool less than two weeks after the project finished.

The notice from the Interior Department said the WWII fountains will receive “new waterproofing,” but makes no mention of a fresh paint job.

A tourist vandalized the memorial in August with spray paint and dish soap. It closed for one day before reopening with no permanent damage.

The WWII Memorial is not the only monument the Trump administration set its sights on in recent weeks.

Earlier this month fences went up around the U.S. Marine Corps War Memorial near Arlington National Cemetery as contractors began cleaning the statue as part of Trump’s efforts to “beautify our nation’s capital,” according to a spokesperson for the National Park Service. That project, of which the scope is unclear, is expected to be completed in early November.

The Park Service did not answer questions about what work is being completed at the Marine Corps Memorial. Photos show the bronze statues have been polished.

The Trump administration has poured millions into restoring several fountains across the District, demolished the East Wing of the White House to make way for a 90,000-square-foot ballroom and continues to push for a 250-foot arch monument to the president just outside of Arlington National Cemetery.

entries.title: Democratic Congressional Candidate Defends Resurfaced Explicit Photos
entries.summary: Chris Gallant, 37, said the photos have no bearing on his ability to serve in Congress.
entries.content:
A Democrat running for a U.S. House seat representing Long Island said he is “not embarrassed or ashamed” after explicit photos resurfaced over the weekend.

Chris Gallant, 37, is vying to unseat Rep. Nick LaLota (R-New York), and said that the photos have no bearing on his ability to serve in Congress.

“I have always been unapologetically me," Gallant, who is openly gay, said in a message to supporters obtained Monday by Newsday. “These attacks on my identity have just made me stronger in my values and convictions."

The photos, which circulated as advertisements for a sex store in San Francisco up until 2020, depict Gallant modeling in a leather posture collar and metal chains. The pictures were first reported by the New York Post. 

“The photographs are authentic and were taken during a private, consensual photo session involving Chris and his then-partner, with whom he was in a committed four-year relationship,” Gallant’s attorney told the Post of his work as a model. “These photographs have no bearing on Chris’s record, qualifications, judgment, or ability to serve.”

Some of the other images date back to 2007 and show Gallant — a retired Army officer and former Black Hawk helicopter pilot — wearing a leather harness and bartending in underwear in Fire Island.

Even before the pictures surfaced, Gallant faced an uphill battle for New York’s 1st Congressional District, which includes parts of Long Island and is rated solid Republican by the Cook Political Report. As of June 30, LaLota has outraised Gallant by over $3 million, according to Federal Election Commission records.

The images have created commotion online, but it remains unclear what role they will play in the race, which remains tight. In January, Public Policy Polling, a Democratic-affiliated polling firm, found Gallant three points behind LaLota, with 20% of voters undecided.

“He will not allow photographs from a past relationship or employment to be distorted and weaponized for political purposes or used to distract voters from the issues that matter," Gallant’s lawyer added.

entries.title: Republican Candidate Doubles Down on the Racist Post Roiling Texas Politics
entries.summary: Bo French dismissed Republican critics like Sen. John Cornyn as “less-conservative people.”
entries.content:
Bo French, the Republican nominee for Texas railroad commissioner, stood by a series of racist social media posts he sent targeting Asian students at the University of Texas, dismissing criticism from fellow Republicans as he campaigns for a seat that oversees the state’s oil and gas industry.

French dismissed the backlash he garnered over his post on X showing a photograph of students celebrating Texas’ football victory over Ohio State, and suggested the students pictured benefitted from discriminatory admissions practices designed to exclude American-born students.

“Social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners” he wrote in a subsequent post. “It’s everywhere and far worse than any of us could imagine.”

French pushed back at those offended by his posts, including U.S. Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), in a Monday radio interview on “The Mark Davis Show.”

“I don’t have anything against the people specifically in that picture,” French told Davis on Monday.

“The establishment raised and spent $7 million against me in the primary,” he added. “Many of the people who criticized me yesterday were some of the same people involved in that effort. It’s no surprise that the less-conservative people in Texas are the ones attacking me.”

French’s original post was quickly corrected in an X community note, which specified that Texas state law requires at least 90% of the university’s freshmen be Texas residents, and that international students comprise about 4% of the school’s newcomers.

Cornyn had urged Republican officials to condemn French’s posts, warning that intolerance and racism should not become normalized.

“This is how great political parties self-destruct. Sad,” he wrote on X.

Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows, a Republican, also decried the posts and called for their removal, saying opposition to immigration policies did not justify disparaging people based on race or ethnicity.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott distanced himself from French’s message, too, while reiterating his support for immigration restrictions.

French is running for the statewide Texas railroad commissioner office, which serves as the primary regulatory body for the state’s massive oil and natural gas industry.

In November, he’s set to face off against Democratic state Rep. Jon Rosenthal, a Houston lawmaker who worked for 25 years as an oil and gas engineer. French defeated the incumbent commissioner, Jim Wright, in May’s Republican runoff.

Rosenthal said in a statement to The Texas Tribune that his campaign saw $35,000 in contributions following French’s remarks.

“Bo French’s own party has said he is unfit for the office he seeks to hold — and Texans are putting their money behind the oil field engineer who is qualified for it,” he said.

Following his talk-radio appearance Monday, French attempted to flip the controversy into a fundraising push for his campaign.

“The radical left and their allies are attacking me,” he wrote on X. “Join the thousands of patriots who are supporting our campaign.”

entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Afternoon Sun newsletter for Sept. 14, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Donald Trump Jr.’s wife, Bettina Anderson, confirmed this morning that a Russian oligarch with ties to President Vladimir Putin bankrolled part of the couple’s wedding weekend in the Bahamas earlier this year.

  • “Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift,” she wrote on Instagram.

John Fetterman’s surprise video at last week’s Republican midterm convention came after organizers sought an “oh shit” moment featuring “walk away” figures from the Democratic party. Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pennsylvania), who has become friends with Fetterman, was the one who secured his involvement.

  • "I want to do it. I’m sure it will make people mad,” Fetterman told McCormick, Axios reported. "But you're my friend, and I want to introduce you.”

Trump is rejecting the idea of new AI regulation, posting Monday that “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”

The detention center known as “Alligator Alcatraz” put immigrants inside small metal cages labeled “calming areas,” according to a report from the Department of Homeland Security inspector general.

The Environmental Protection Agency is repealing limits on greenhouse gas emissions created by coal- and natural-gas-fueled power plants.

The National Weather Service announced this morning that it would change the name of Lake Ontario on its maps and forecasts to use Trump’s preferred “Lake America” moniker.

A second federal judge blocked the Trump administration from implementing a U.S. Postal Service rule that would tighten mail-in voting requirements.

States, cities and counties filed two lawsuits today challenging federal rules that would allow immigrants’ use of public benefits to be considered in applications to enter the country such as green cards.

A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to turn over thousands of internal USAID records sought by The Washington Sun (Hey, that’s us!).

Former Sen. Joe Manchin (D-West Virginia) endorsed Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) in her close race for reelection, calling his longtime legislative partner the “soul of the Senate.”

  • "I have always been unapologetically me," Gallant, who is openly gay, said. "These attacks on my identity have just made me stronger in my values and convictions."

entries.title: Congress Is About to Do a Whole Lot of Nothing About AI
entries.summary: Top tech CEOs are raising alarms about the escalating threat of rapid development but Capitol Hill leaders are resisting quick action.
entries.content:
Tech leaders are begging Congress to step in and provide guardrails on AI development after dire warnings about the rapid advances in the technology and its risks to humanity, but lawmakers remain as divided as ever on how and whether to do so.

“We do not want to jump in,” House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Monday. “The reflex of legislative bodies is to cover things up with red tape and hyper-regulation. If you do that, then you lose your edge, and that is a national security concern for the American people,” he said, arguing the United States must stay ahead of China in the AI race.

Johnson said President Donald Trump was summoning officials and tech leaders to a meeting at the White House late this week or early next, but Trump has already declared flat-out opposition to new laws regulating AI.

In a Monday post on his social media website Truth Social, Trump said “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" He added that there “is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”

Last week, several Anthropic researchers warned about the existential threat posed by AI, with one going so far as putting the risk of humanity’s extinction at greater than 10%. Top AI leaders including ChatGPT founder Sam Altman, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, are also raising unprecedented warnings about the pace of development, calling for an immediate slowdown in advancing AI models.

Democrats argue legislation is needed to curb frontier AI development and put in oversight measures like independent evaluators to ensure the technology is kept in check and doesn’t go rogue like in several recent incidents. Many fear AI will enable sophisticated cyberattacks or aid the development of biological or nuclear weapons.

The Republican-controlled Congress doesn’t appear set to take meaningful action anytime soon. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is planning a caucus meeting on AI on Tuesday, while Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is pressing the Trump administration to hold a classified briefing for members of the Senate on the risks posed by AI.

“Warning bells are ringing louder than they ever have – and the Trump administration is looking the other way,” Schumer said in a statement on Monday. “Well, if they won’t hold themselves accountable, we will.”

Past meetings and briefings with top tech leaders have yielded little progress on AI, even when Democrats were in power.

In September 2023, for example, Schumer, who was Senate majority leader at the time, convened a bipartisan group of senators for a closed-door meeting on AI with top tech leaders, including Musk and Altman. Musk warned lawmakers at the time about the "civilizational risk" posed by AI, and voiced support for a standalone federal agency to regulate AI. The senators later released a roadmap for AI regulation aiming to balance technological growth with essential guardrails, but it went nowhere.

Democrats responded to last week’s warnings by calling for emergency action on AI, though there’s not much time to do so. The Senate is scheduled to be in session for three weeks before leaving town to allow senators to campaign ahead of the November midterm elections. The House is scheduled to be in session only for one week before doing the same.

“Congress should be on an emergency footing in the coming week,” said Hawaii Sen. Brian Schatz. “We have to move at the pace of the threat, not our own habits and rhythms. People are depending on us to take swift bipartisan action that meaningfully reduces AI risk.”

Senators are set to consider legislation this week regulating crypto and college sports. The House, meanwhile, is expected to vote on bipartisan legislation sanctioning Russia over its war in Ukraine.

Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, has called for a moratorium on data center construction and a halt on advanced AI development. He also introduced legislation to ban AI superintelligence, but no Senate Democrats have joined him on that measure.

Other Democrats favor a less aggressive approach, proposing safety measures while allowing for AI development to continue.

Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal wrote in a post online that a voluntary system of auditors was not enough, referring to tech leaders’ vows to institute internal safeguard. “It must be a statutorily established regimen, with power to determine whether models & new products are safe & effective, just as independent scientists are authorized to do under the FDA,” he said.

One measure that could gain traction is being written by Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz, who chairs the Senate Commerce Committee, which has jurisdiction over technology issues. Cruz has been working alongside Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota). The bill has not yet been publicly released, but Cruz said its goal is to “address catastrophic risks involving biological or nuclear threats” associated with AI.

“We cannot stick our heads in the sand and pretend this technology isn’t happening. We need guardrails,” Cruz wrote online. “But America needs to lead. If China leads the world in AI, the whole world is in trouble.”

Sen. Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the commerce committee, appeared to signal concerns with the bill over the weekend, noting Republicans attempted to pass a 10-year ban on state AI regulation in last year's tax-cut law.

“I welcome the urgency,” Cantwell wrote last week “But the answer is not a weak federal standard that becomes a backdoor for wiping out stronger state protections.”

In the House, lawmakers have introduced the Frontier Act, which would create a national framework for overseeing AI development, and the AI Kill Switch Act, which would require developers to maintain the ability to pause or shut down advanced AI systems.

With Congress mired in gridlock for the immediate future, however, the responsibility of slowing AI development will rest primarily with AI companies themselves.

In a midnight post on X on Sunday, Altman said his support for slowing AI development doesn’t mean stopping it outright. He also urged the U.S. and China to work together to address risks posed by the technology.

“Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs,” he said.

“Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring,” he added. “Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.”

entries.title: National Weather Service Orders Staff to Use ‘Lake America’ in Future Forecasts
entries.summary: The agency has already changed the names of several geographical features to reflect President Donald Trump’s decisions.
entries.content:
The U.S. agency that provides weather forecasts and warnings to the public is implementing President Donald Trump’s name change for Lake Ontario, now dubbed “Lake America.”

The National Weather Service, which is part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, announced on Monday that “work is underway to update naming conventions as quickly as possible on online maps, weather products, websites and other materials across the NWS,” in accordance with Trump’s executive order on the lake.

The NWS and the NOAA are in turn part of the Department of Commerce, and all executive branch agencies are required to follow any presidential orders.

The NWS already uses “Gulf of America” instead of the Gulf of Mexico and “Mount McKinley” instead of Denali, reflecting Trump’s previous efforts to rename bodies of water and geographical landmarks to “honor American greatness” — without securing congressional approval.

The U.S. Geological Survey, a science and mapping agency inside the Department of the Interior, also changed its maps to reflect “Lake America.”

Lake Ontario sits on the border between the U.S. and Canada, and the two countries have been locked in an escalating trade war.

“I find Canada to be the worst country to deal with,” Trump told reporters Sunday on Air Force One. “With that being said, they’re dying to make a deal.”

When asked about Canada’s willingness to make a deal, Prime Minister Mark Carney told Bloomberg, "I'd say what we've been saying all along, which is that there is a mutually advantageous agreement that's possible between Canada and the United States," adding that he welcomes the Trump’s comments and he is ready to “sit down and negotiate.”

Carney appears willing to work through trade talks with the U.S. despite Trump’s push to change the name of their shared body of water, but Ontario Premier Doug Ford has taken a much harder line against the president.

Ford erected a large, two-story billboard last month that says “Lake Ontario Now and Always” in Grimsby, a Canadian city on the shore of the lake.

“Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario,” Ford said standing in front of the billboard in a video posted to X on Aug. 29.
