entries.title: Despite Its Success, the Spirit Can’t Seem to Find the Back of the Net
entries.summary: Second-place Washington was shut out Sunday for the third time in its last five home matches.
entries.content:
Not long after the disastrous final moments of Sunday’s meeting with Boston Legacy FC, in which a narrow 1-0 deficit ballooned to a 3-0 loss in a matter of minutes, Washington Spirit midfielder Hal Hershfelt reflected on her team’s apparent inability to put the ball in the back of the net.

“I feel like a lot of our goals are from individual brilliance, because we have individually brilliant players,” Hershfelt said. “But I feel like it's getting to that point in the season where teams are figuring that out. We need to mix it up and work with each other in attacking moments.”

The Spirit entered Sunday’s game with plenty to feel good about. After a tough August stretch saw Washington go four games without a win, coach Adrián González’s team seemed to be getting back on track with back-to-back victories. It entered the weekend sitting in second place in the National Women’s Soccer League table, only two points behind Gotham FC in the race for the NWSL Shield. Boston came to D.C. in 14th place with the league’s third-worst defense, a perfect visitor for a team looking to maintain momentum.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Instead, the Spirit’s recent attacking troubles were on display again as it struggled to create any clear-cut scoring opportunities in front of an eager home crowd at Audi Field. With the loss, Washington (13-7-4) fell five points behind Gotham and back into the thick of a tight playoff seeding race.

The Spirit’s only real chances came late in Sunday’s match, after Aïssata Traoré gave Boston a lead in the 81st minute. Not only did the Spirit fail to find an equalizer, it gave up a stoppage-time brace to Amanda Gutierres to seal the team’s worst home defeat since April 2025.

“We need to be better, of course, especially attacking-wise, connecting and trying to create chances,” González said. “Tough one, but as always, good learning. And I do prefer this now than obviously [at the] end of the season or in a potential playoff. We need to learn, we need to be humble and we need to accept it.”

The Spirit struggled to maintain possession while attempting to play through Boston’s press, and when it was able to get forward and find players in dangerous positions, they couldn’t execute the final ball. Washington produced just three shots on target, all of which were straight at experienced Boston goalkeeper Casey Murphy, and was shut out for third time in its last five games at Audi Field.

“They were very patient in a high block, and we probably didn't shift them left to right as much as we could have done to then open them up,” defender Esme Morgan said. “The moments where we did and we were able to find players in the pocket or Hal through the six, we were then able to progress a bit better, but then didn't really capitalize on those moments.”

Washington’s 33 goals in 24 league games is only the ninth-most of 16 NWSL teams, and its attacking output has slowed, with just 11 goals in its last 11 matches. The Spirit has been heavily reliant on Trinity Rodman to score and create goals this year and has struggled recently with other key attacking options out injured and a few newcomers forced into bigger roles.

Rodman is already up to 10 league goals and six assists, accounting for nearly half of the attacking production for a team that’s boasted a broader distribution of scoring in recent years — no individual player has notched more than 10 NWSL goals in a season for the Spirit since Crystal Dunn scored 15 times in 2015.

Forward Sofia Cantore and midfielder Leicy Santos have both netted five NWSL goals this year while midfielder Rebeca Bernal, who joined Manchester United on a transfer earlier this month, and forward Claudia Martínez, who returned on Sunday after missing two games with a lower leg injury, have scored three times. Defender Tara Rudd is the only other Spirit player to score multiple NWSL goals this year.

Despite the team’s scoring woes, González has still seen Washington get into dangerous positions in recent weeks and believes the team knows how to play to its strengths.

“Right now we are not in a momentum where you need to change the way that you create chances or you need to start implementing new things,” González said “Of course, we are always open, but I think it's a matter of knowing what we have and just exploring that.”

While the Spirit got into positive areas at times on Sunday, specifically early in the match when winning the ball high up the pitch, finding the back of the net has proven to be a challenge, especially while bringing new players into the fold and managing the return of others, like Martínez and Ashley Hatch, an experienced attacking option.

Monique Ngock and Mélissa Bethi, who joined the Spirit this summer from French league sides Fleury Merogis U.S. and Nantes, respectively, earned their second starts for their new club in midfield and have shown individual moments of quality — especially Bethi, who scored the 80th-minute winner against Portland and won a penalty kick in the 70th minute against Boston that was overturned after video review — but the duo still need time to develop chemistry with their new teammates.

“They're great players, and they give us a lot in the midfield and in an attack, but sometimes maybe they're not on the same page as the people who have been here for years,” Rudd said of Ngock and Bethi. “Those relationships come in training and playing together and knowing each other on the field and what your tendencies are.”

Washington also recently signed 21-year-old Tanzanian striker Clara Luvanga from Saudi Arabian side Al Nassr to a four-year contract, a move that could bolster its front line.

The Spirit doesn’t have an endless amount of time to form new connections as it approaches the business end of the season, but Washington remains in a strong position in the league table with six regular season games remaining. The Spirit will have a great opportunity to bounce back on Sunday when the team travels to take on the last-place Chicago Stars, who have conceded a league-high 54 goals in 24 games this season.

entries.title: A Military Official Says U.S. Has Put ‘Space Control Weapons’ in Orbit
entries.summary: It marks the first public acknowledgment of space-based capabilities previously kept under wraps.
entries.content:
The U.S. military has deployed weapons into orbit, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Monday, publicly acknowledging a capability in space that the Pentagon had kept largely secret.

“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink said at the Air & Space Forces Association’s annual conference in National Harbor, Maryland, according to DefenseScoop. “This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary actions.”

Meink did not say what the weapons are, how many are in orbit or what they can do. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, the Space Force said, “Space control requires both offensive and defensive actions,” including operations to disrupt, degrade, deny or destroy an adversary’s counterspace capabilities and actions to protect U.S. systems from attack.

The Space Force declined to say when the weapons were deployed, whether they are kinetic or non-kinetic, or to provide other details about the systems.

But Meink made clear that the disclosure was deliberate. Asked about the statement after his speech, Meink said his wording was “very well thought out,” according to Air & Space Forces Magazine.

Meink’s statement appears to be the first time the Pentagon has publicly acknowledged that the U.S. military has weapons operating in orbit.

Space Force officials had previously said they planned to field a “substantial on-orbit capability” by 2026. Senior military leaders have also openly called for putting weapons and interceptors in space. But until Monday, officials had stopped short of saying weapons were already there.

The disclosure follows a broader shift by the Space Force toward talking publicly about how it would fight in space.

In a warfighting framework released last year, the service laid out how U.S. forces could protect American satellites and disable or destroy an adversary’s systems. Those attacks could physically damage a satellite or use electronic or cyber capabilities to disrupt it or cut off its communications.

It is not clear whether the weapons Meink disclosed Monday can do any of those things.

U.S. officials have repeatedly pointed to China and Russia as the main threats driving the military buildup in space. The Space Force says both countries are developing ways to attack or disrupt American satellites, including missiles, jammers, lasers and systems placed in orbit.

Meink separately highlighted the Space-Based Interceptor program, which is being developed as part of President Donald Trump’s Golden Dome missile-defense system.

The interceptors are still under development. The Space Force is building a network of interceptors in low-Earth orbit and says it plans to demonstrate an initial capability integrated with Golden Dome in 2028.

entries.title: Mahmoud Khalil Sues Columbia Over Its Treatment of Pro-Palestinian Activists
entries.summary: Khalil's lawsuit says Columbia “refused to correct disinformation” about him while he was detained by immigration enforcement.
entries.content:
By Sudhin Thanawala

Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil sued Columbia University on Monday, alleging it failed to address harassment against him and other members of a pro-Palestinian campus group and retaliated against them when they reported it.

The university's “deliberate indifference” led to the doxing of multiple group members and Khalil’s detention by immigration agents, according to the civil rights lawsuit filed in federal court in New York City.

The university declined to comment on the lawsuit, but said in an email that “creating a campus environment where every member of our community feels welcome, supported, and safe is fundamental to who we are as a University.”

“Columbia is committed to protecting our community from discrimination and harassment, and responding promptly and appropriately when concerns arise,” it said.

Khalil also sued Columbia last year to block the release of student records to a congressional committee.

A former graduate student at Columbia University, Khalil gained prominence as a spokesperson for student activists protesting Israel's actions in Gaza.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested him at his campus apartment in March 2025, and he quickly became the face of the Trump administration's crackdown on pro-Palestinian demonstrators.

Khalil spent 104 days in a Louisiana immigration jail, missing the birth of his first child, before a federal judge in New Jersey ordered his release. His deportation case remains active.

Khalil's lawsuit says Columbia “refused to correct disinformation” about him while he was detained, “allowing a false narrative about his conduct and role to persist and further enabling peer-on-peer harassment of other Palestinian students and students with perceived shared Arab and/or Muslim ancestry.”

Instead of investigating reports of harassment, the university retaliated by characterizing events by a pro-Palestinian campus group as security risks and revising disciplinary policy to target criticism of the Israeli government, according to the lawsuit.

It accuses Columbia of civil rights violations, requests a court order restoring Khalil's access to the campus and ending the Palestinian group's suspension, and seeks damages “to be determined at trial.”

It also names the pro-Palestinian group and its president, Mohammad Zubairi, as plaintiffs.

entries.title: Supreme Court Halts Postal Service From Using Trump’s Mail-In Ballot Rule
entries.summary: The decision allows states to continue their current processes for voting through the mail.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court on Monday halted the U.S. Postal Service from going forward with a rule pushed by the Trump administration to restrict and change the process for mailing ballots in November’s election.

The 7-2 decision clears the way for states to use mail ballots under their current process, avoiding last-minute requirements that some election officials said would disenfranchise voters. Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented.

The high court sided with voting rights groups and nearly half the states, which said it would cause a mad scramble for states to comply and, in some cases, it would be impossible within the timeframe of an election now 50 days away.

“Applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections,” Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in his opinion Monday.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to lift a lower court ruling that blocked key parts of the USPS rule through Election Day on Nov. 3.

The rule stems from an executive order President Donald Trump signed in March that sought to redefine the federal government’s role in the mail-in ballot process. The president has said the policies will help safeguard elections from noncitizen voting — though noncitizen registration is illegal and rare, according to experts.

The rule requires states to submit the name, address and a unique barcode number of every eligible voter to a USPS portal, and then check that each outgoing ballot matches an entry on that list.

The USPS said in its final rule that each outgoing ballot envelope must be scanned individually, with a member of election staff present to oversee the entire process.

It also included an approval process for ballot envelopes, which many states have already purchased for their primaries, along with upgrading systems to comply with a new Intelligent Mail barcode, or IMb, for every ballot.

Postal officials previously told The Washington Sun that USPS was rushing its new mailed ballot system without proper testing, which could produce widespread errors and result in disenfranchisement.
entries.author: Adora Brown, Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: Judge Blocks Trump Rule Limiting Student Visas to Four Years
entries.summary: Massachusetts Judge Dennis Saylor called the government’s justification for the new rule “absurd.”
entries.content:
A federal judge in Massachusetts has temporarily blocked the Trump administration's attempt to impose a four-year limit on student visas, granting a preliminary injunction one day before the new rules were set to start.

Judge Dennis Saylor, who was appointed by George W. Bush, called the Department of Homeland Security’s rationale for the new rule "exceptionally weak" in a Monday ruling.

“The government’s contention that the rule is necessary to safeguard national security

borders on the absurd,” he wrote. “It is based almost entirely on a small handful of anecdotes, each of which involved incidents that the new rule would do nothing to prevent or even mitigate.”

The new federal rule by DHS aims to place a strict four-year limit on standard student visas. Immigration officials were set to begin enforcing the new guidelines on Tuesday.

In July, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the policy change would stop foreign students from abusing a “loophole” in the immigration system of “perpetually enrolling in courses to avoid having to leave the U.S.”

A coalition of universities, educators and labor organizations sued DHS in August to stop the rule from taking effect.

Since 1978, Saylor wrote, the United States has issued student visas to foreign students as long as they followed routine immigration rules and made normal progress toward their education goals.

“That system — which has been in place for nearly half a century — has permitted tens of millions of foreign students and researchers to come to the United States. It has also resulted in groundbreaking research in science, medicine, and technology, substantial economic growth, and a host of other benefits, often on a vast scale,” Saylor wrote.

DHS did not immediately respond to The Washington Sun’s request for comment.

entries.title: Thune’s Texas PAC Drops a Whopping $54 Million for Paxton’s Senate Race
entries.summary: The media buy is split between propping up Ken Paxton and opposing James Talarico.
entries.content:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s political action committee dropped a massive $53.9 million investment into the Texas Senate race, according to a Federal Election Commission filing submitted Monday.

The investment from Texas PAC, a committee associated with Thune’s Senate Leadership Fund, divided the media spending push: Nearly $27 million will be used to support Republican nominee Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general, while $27 million is set to oppose Democratic candidate James Talarico, a state lawmaker.

The Texas Tribune reported Friday that Texas PAC purchased $51.3 million in broadcast TV ads in the Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, San Antonio and Austin media markets, citing the media tracking firm AdImpact.

This cash from Thune’s group is the largest single independent expenditure for any candidate so far this cycle. Talarico has been outraising Paxton for months, but Thune’s spending campaign could help Paxton ahead of November’s election.

On Sunday, Texas PAC — which registered through the FEC in late August — made its first $6.6 million investment in the state’s Senate race, with a combination of media and texting buys.

Thune originally endorsed Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) over Paxton in the Senate primary, and groups linked to Thune spent heavily to fend off Cornyn’s primary challengers. Once Paxton won the nomination, however, Thune backed him and has urged President Donald Trump, who made a late primary endorsement for Paxton, to use his funds in the general election campaign.

“All of our allies out there, including the president and his team and their resources, need to be brought to bear on Texas, because it’s not one that we can lose if we’re going to hang on to a Republican majority,” Thune said Sept. 1 on Fox News.

"We are certainly hopeful that the president and his team at MAGA Inc. will be engaged in some of these races," Thune said.

Asked Monday about the influx of money from Thune’s PAC into this one Senate race, Cornyn said: “Well, I mean, obviously, that's their prerogative.”

“At some point, I think you know, given scarce resources, they're going to have to figure out where the money is going to do the most good, and it may or may not be a place like as big and as expensive as Texas,” Cornyn said.

MAGA Inc., the president’s influential super PAC, spent more than $10 million on an ad buy for the Texas Senate race earlier this month in the committee’s first expenditure of the general election.

Thune’s political committee has now spent in every major battleground Senate race, while Trump’s has spent in all but one: It has yet to report dropping significant money in Maine.

entries.title: Whistleblower Says DHS’s Hunt for Unlawful Voting May Have Broken State Laws
entries.summary: Senate Democrats release a report that says immigration officers got little training and “magic” data when looking for noncitizen voters.
entries.content:
Immigration officers are potentially violating state laws about voter data and using unreliable information to create law enforcement records stating that naturalized U.S. citizens voted before obtaining citizenship, according to a new whistleblower report.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Alex Padilla (D-California) made the complaint public Monday and said it raises concerns about the accuracy of the Department of Homeland Security’s probe into immigration-related election fraud.

The unidentified whistleblower is a public servant with direct knowledge of the Unlawful Voter Initiative launched in August, according to the report the Democracy Defenders Fund submitted to the lawmakers last week.

Immigration officers working for the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services were tasked with finding out whether immigrants and naturalized citizens voted illegally. They were trained to do so by claiming to be the subjects of the investigation or acting on their behalf on state government websites, a potential violation of state laws, according to the report.

“The Whistleblower reports that given the nature of the Initiative, the pressures put on officers, and the instructions given by headquarters, it is likely the case that no officer who has sought to access information on a state website has been truthful about his or her identity,” the report states. “The Unlawful Voter Initiative includes all 50 states and is targeted at up to hundreds of thousands of individuals.”

A White House spokesperson referred questions to DHS. The department and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Officers received a video training on Aug. 21 and were required to begin the probe on Aug. 25, with an assigned quota of at least five reviews per hour, according to the report, meaning employees had roughly 12 minutes to determine each case.

The video training said some information that wasn’t in the source data for the investigations would be "brought in through supplemental magic,” according to the whistleblower complaint. “Magic is not a recognized form of record keeping under state or federal law,” it notes.

DHS has been touting arrests of immigrants it claims illegally voted.

The investigation swept in naturalized citizens, regardless of how recent their contact with DHS had been, the whistleblower report says. “It is irrelevant if a subject naturalized decades ago, has no current applications with USCIS, or even if they’re deceased,” the report states. “All that matters is that the DHS source data indicates that they are a subject with an alien number that registered to vote or voted.”

Schumer described the report as a “bombshell whistleblower complaint” in a Monday press conference.

“The length Trump will go to cheat, lie and steal in this upcoming election are simply beyond the pale,” Schumer said. “Apparently, agents are being commanded to violate state laws to access private voter information and fabricate law enforcement records as part of DHS's ‘unlawful voter initiative.’”

Another whistleblower complaint released this month outlined the U.S. Postal Service’s plans to implement President Donald Trump’s mail-in ballot restrictions. The complaint said this could result in millions of voters not getting ballots or receiving them late.

entries.title: McConnell Returns to Senate Vowing to Be Present for 'Tough Votes'
entries.summary: The former Senate majority leader has been out since June and admitted Monday, “I’m still not quite back to 100%."
entries.content:
Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky returned to the Capitol on Monday after a roughly three-month absence.

He announced his plans in a post on X, saying he was looking forward to seeing his colleagues.

“My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process, and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven’t made it any easier. I’m still not quite back to 100%, but I’ve assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me.”

The Kentucky Republican, who arrived in a wheelchair Monday evening, greeted reporters saying, "I'm glad to see you, time to get back to work.”

McConnell has not appeared at the Capitol since he suffered a medical incident at his home in Washington, D.C., on June 14.

The longtime Senate Republican leader spent roughly four weeks at the hospital following a fall and a subsequent pneumonia diagnosis. He went to a rehabilitation center in mid-July for physical therapy, his office said at the time.

He was discharged from the rehab center in early August.

“Earlier today, I was discharged from the rehabilitation center to continue my recovery at home,” McConnell said in a statement at the time. “On the advice of my doctors, I’ll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period, and I’ll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business.”

McConnell has been inundated with questions about his future and his health status during the past three months, including from Kentucky's Democratic governor, Andy Beshear. McConnell's team has released two photos of him alongside his wife, former Transportation Secretary Elaine Chao.

This is a breaking story and will be updated.
entries.author: Reese Gorman

entries.title: Newsom Says He Won’t Challenge Harris if She Runs in 2028
entries.summary: The California governor said a primary battle against Harris would be a “gift from God” for political opponents.
entries.content:
Gov. Gavin Newsom will not run in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris decides to make another bid for the presidency.

Widely considered a top contender to become the next Democratic nominee for president, the California governor told CNN that a contest between him and Harris “doesn’t make sense.”

“I wouldn't run if she ran,” Newsom said. “I know her base of supporters. I know her friends. The Venn diagram on that is just pure crossover. … I wouldn't do that to people.”

Newsom has laid miles of groundwork for a 2028 presidential campaign, recently visiting early primary and battleground states like South Carolina, in a “take it back” tour to rally base voters and confront Republican policies.

He’s also positioned himself as a reliable Democratic surrogate, and has participated in media appearances to cement himself as an ideological foil to MAGA Republicans, including a televised debate against Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis.

Newsom said Monday contesting Harris for the nomination would be “a gift from God” to his political opponents.

“They’d enjoy the hell out of it — mutual assured destruction,” he said. “It services no greater good.”

Harris ran unsuccessfully for the presidency in 2020 and again in 2024 after then-President Joe Biden dropped out of his reelection bid.

Correction: Kamala Harris ran for president in 2020 and 2024. A previous version of this story included a wrong year.

entries.title: Brennan Attorney Says DOJ Is Running ‘Multiple’ Probes Into Trump Foes
entries.summary: Court filing from the former CIA director’s attorney says he was told a “far reaching” investigation includes “issues at Mar-a-Lago and beyond.”
entries.content:
The Justice Department is running not one but several criminal investigations into President Donald Trump’s political enemies, according to a court filing by former CIA director John Brennan’s attorney.

That includes a federal grand jury run out of a tiny satellite federal courthouse in Fort Pierce, Florida, where Brennan is being required to testify next month. But a new declaration filed by Brennan defense attorney Kenneth Wainstein says a Trump administration official told him there were “multiple ‘viable’ grand jury investigations.”

Wainstein’s filing noted that Kurt Olsen is taking a leading role in the investigation — meaning Olsen, a MAGA loyalist who helped Trump challenge 2020 election results by presenting conspiracy theories, is likely preparing to relitigate that election.

“Mr. Olsen fielded our inquiries and indicated there are multiple ‘viable’ grand jury investigations, including a ‘far-reaching’ investigation in Fort Pierce that includes ‘issues at Mar-a-Lago and beyond’ into whether President Trump had his civil rights violated,” Wainstein wrote.

The declaration was filed as part of Brennan’s lawsuit in D.C., where he’s asking a federal judge to order that the DOJ keep every shred of paper or email documenting the ongoing prosecution — with the expectation that the former CIA director will need it to defend himself in court.

Wainstein’s declaration says that Olsen’s comments about the nature of the investigation came up during a Sept. 11 conference call, with Brennan’s two defense lawyers on one end of the call and Olsen and three other members of the prosecution team on the other.

Olsen’s description of investigators’ interest in Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s Palm Beach resort, indicates two things: that the government is using its location to launch the investigation in South Florida, and that former special counsel Jack Smith’s decision to have the FBI raid the house is part of the case.

The only sitting judge in the Fort Pierce courthouse is U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, who was appointed by Trump during his first term and later dismissed the criminal indictment against him filed by Smith months before the 2024 election that sent Trump back to the White House.

Prosecutors also appeared to tell Brennan’s lawyers that the former CIA director is a “target” of a narrower inquiry, but that he’s merely a “subject” of the “more wide-ranging conspiracy,” Wainstein’s filing states. However, the smaller investigation was portrayed as potentially a part of the larger one, creating a confusing distinction.

The revelations from Wainstein, who once oversaw the creation of the DOJ’s National Security Division, shed light on parts of what portends to be a wide-ranging effort by the Trump administration to exact vengeance on former government leaders. Trump has long held those leaders personally responsible for tainting his first term with politically motivated investigations into his alleged criminal ties to Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

Wainstein also provided a window into the chaos in the ongoing DOJ criminal probes, noting that the investigations continue despite the sudden departure last week of Joseph diGenova, a Trump loyalist who had been overseeing the effort.

According to Wainstein’s filing, diGenova signed the subpoena for Brennan’s testimony on Wednesday, and the government emailed it to Brennan’s lawyer on Thursday. But when Wainstein texted diGenova about it that same morning, diGenova responded that he would “arrange counsel” to speak to Brennan’s lawyer.

Within hours, news broke that diGenova had quit — telling the New York Post that “if you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem.”

Several sources have told The Washington Sun that the ongoing probes involved an FBI unit known colloquially as the “payback squad” but carries the formal designation “Director’s Advisory Team.” According to these sources, the team includes John Charles Eckenrode, who once worked on special counsel John Durham’s probe into the origins of the Trump-Russia investigation, and FBI special agent Rosemaria Vasiliki Marketos, who was passed up for Jack Smith’s special counsel team and has repeated Trump’s oft-disproven conspiracy theories about the 2020 election being stolen.

In the D.C. case, Brennan’s lawyers made clear when they sued on July 1 that they will fight any criminal charges by pointing to evidence that he “is being vindictively singled out for investigation and prosecution.”

“Given these strong indicia of vindictiveness, Director Brennan expects that he will forcefully challenge any eventual indictment as the product of an unconstitutionally vindictive and selective prosecution,” they wrote in their complaint.

In court papers, the DOJ has called Brennan’s attempt an “unprecedented step of managing potential discovery” in what it called “a hypothetical future criminal case in Florida.” Prosecutors also dodged any discussion of Brennan’s concerns that the Trump administration deliberately chose to pursue criminal charges in Cannon’s courthouse — far from where most of the actions in question took place in Washington, D.C.

“The government declines to engage with speculative allegations of judge-shopping regarding a hypothetical indictment,” Jeremy Newman, the chief litigation counsel at the DOJ’s civil division, responded July 28.

entries.title: Trump Calls Into a Tech Conference to Declare AI Warnings a 'Hoax'
entries.summary: The president rejected mounting fears that AI could spiral out of control.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump unexpectedly called into a business and technology conference through Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s cell phone and dismissed urgent warnings from those inside the artificial intelligence industry as a “hoax.”

Trump called Huang, who has previously dismissed growing concerns about AI, while he appeared at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles on Monday.

“The robots will not be taking over,” Trump said to the crowd after Huang put the call on speaker. “The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax.”

“We have to do things, and we have to do it prudently. But that doesn't mean we're going to stop an industry,” Trump added.

Trump appeared pleased that Huang shared his convictions about the AI industry.

During his brief call, the president doubled down on his view that the U.S. must not lose the AI development race to China. Nvidia, a large tech company that develops computer chips used in AI models, has found itself in the center of the tech race between the U.S. and China as each country tries to lead in the emerging field.

“We're going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race in America,” Huang said.

Trump also called for protecting data centers alongside his call to safeguard AI from those trying to slow the pace of the developments.

“Data centers are great, and they make people wealthy,” Trump said.

The president has cast aside dire warnings from tech developers, industry leaders and lawmakers calling for the U.S. government to address the dangers of AI.

Both House and Senate lawmakers plan to discuss and focus on AI this week. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) will be joining forces with former Trump White House adviser Steve Bannon on Tuesday to push for “human-controlled AI,” Axios reported.

Earlier on Monday, Trump said he is the only “control or ‘guardrails’” needed for the industry and again pointed to what he deemed a “SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind Chair Demis Hassabis and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk have all called for independent oversight on AI and slowing development.

Amodei published an essay on Saturday calling for companies to partner with the federal government, which he said could serve as an “evaluator” that implements safety regulations or as a mediator between tech corporations in the process of establishing standards.

The mounting concern over AI spiraling out of control as a result of the race between the industry leaders came to a head when Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, quit his job and took to social media to issue an urgent warning.

Coxon told The Washington Sun that he felt like he was “contributing to the potential death race” through his work.

Anthropic’s alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, backed up Coxon’s warning, writing that he believed the company “is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.”
